items.claim: On any AEM instance the /api.json path is worth poisoning with Host, X-Forwarded-Server and X-Forwarded-Host (or a localhost Host value) to see whether an attacker-controlled host value ends up in a cached response.
items.body:
On any AEM instance the /api.json path is worth poisoning with Host, X-Forwarded-Server and X-Forwarded-Host (or a localhost Host value) to see whether an attacker-controlled host value ends up in a cached response.

HackTricks reference: host header (https://kathan19.gitbook.io/howtohunt/host-header-attack/host-header.md)
items.disproof: None of those headers is reflected into the response body or stored in a cache entry, and cache keys vary so no poisoned value is ever served to another user.

sources.quote:
If you come across /api.json in any AEM instance during bug hunting, try for web cache poisoning via following\
 Host: , X-Forwarded-Server , X-Forwarded-Host: and or simply try <https://localhost/api.json> HTTP/1.1
4.

An interception proxy is particularly vulnerable if it relies on the host and port information for redirecting requests to internal servers, or for use as a cache key in a shared cache, without first verifying that the intercepted connection is targeting a valid IP address for that host.
Reflected, client-side vulnerabilities, such as XSS, are typically not exploitable when they're caused by the Host header. There is no way for an attacker to force a victim's browser
